lesson.title: Your connected project
lesson.subtitle: From a problem near you to a design others can judge

video.title: Your connected project
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside a photo-style drawing of a low concrete bridge under brown floodwater, a minibus stuck halfway, passengers safe on the bank.
scenes.animation: Rain streaks; the water line rises on the bridge posts.
scenes.narration: Every rainy season, the road to Musa's school floods at the low bridge. Last year a minibus drove in and got stuck. Nobody was hurt, but nobody had known how deep the water was.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: turn a problem in your community into a connected design.

scenes.visual: Students talking with a minibus driver and a mother at the roadside; a notebook page fills with their answers and a boxed goal.
scenes.animation: Speech bubbles pop; the goal box draws round the last line.
scenes.narration: Good projects start with a problem and the people who have it, not with a gadget. Ask them what goes wrong, when, and who gets hurt. Then write what success looks like: nobody drives into deep water again.

scenes.visual: The bridge again, now with a depth sensor on a post, a small box beside it, a flashing amber light, and a radio wave reaching a driver's phone in town.
scenes.animation: Each part lights up in turn as it is named.
scenes.narration: Every connected design has four parts. Sense: a sensor measures the water's depth. Decide: a small computer checks if it's too deep. Act: a warning light flashes. Connect: a message warns drivers before they set off.

scenes.visual: Three design cards side by side, each with a small sketch: a lamp on a post; a lamp and a phone with a text bubble; a camera with a video stream to a phone.
scenes.animation: Cards slide in one by one.
scenes.narration: There's always more than one design. First, a flashing light at the bridge, with no network. Second, the light plus text alerts to drivers' phones. Third, a camera streaming live video of the bridge to an app.

scenes.visual: Four weighing pans in a row, each labelled with an icon: coins, a battery under a cloud, a shield, an eye.
scenes.animation: Each pan dips as it is named.
scenes.narration: Weigh every design on the same things. Cost: can people afford it, and fix it? Power: will it last a cloudy week? Safety: what happens when it fails? Privacy: does it watch people who never agreed?

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor beside the bridge drawing; the sensor on the post shows a crack and a question mark. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The water sensor at the bridge breaks during a storm. What should the warning light do?

scenes.visual: Two versions side by side: a dark lamp with a minibus heading for the water (red cross); a flashing lamp with the minibus stopping, and a phone showing 'sensor needs repair'.
scenes.animation: The dark lamp gets a red cross; the flashing lamp a green check.
scenes.narration: Flash, and report it. A dark light tells drivers it's safe: the most dangerous message of all. Good designs fail safe: when they can't tell, they warn.

scenes.visual: A score table becomes a bar chart: the light with text alerts is tallest, the light alone close behind, the camera far lower.
scenes.animation: Bars grow one by one; the winner gets a star.
scenes.narration: Now score each design from one to five on each thing, and agree with the people affected how much each matters. Here, safety counts most. The light with text alerts wins: cheap, low power, early warnings, and it films nobody.

scenes.visual: A student pins a poster on the classroom wall: problem, a four-box drawing, a score table and a risks list; a driver and a parent read it and point.
scenes.animation: Poster sections appear in turn; sticky notes with questions pop on.
scenes.narration: Last, present your design so others can judge and improve it: the problem, your drawing, your scores, and what could go wrong. Then ask the people it's for: what did we miss?

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside Grace's poster; a minibus waits at the roadside. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Grace's design scores best, but she never asked the minibus drivers about it. What should she do before building it?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a flag, the four-box flow, a balance, a poster with sticky notes.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Ask the drivers first: the people it's for know what your scores miss. Remember: start from a real problem, then sense, decide, act and connect. Weigh designs on cost, power, safety and privacy. Then share it, and improve it.

scenes.visual: A student at a kitchen table with a notebook: four boxes joined by arrows, a small score table, and a family member leaning in to look.
scenes.animation: Boxes draw in; a sticky note with a question appears.
scenes.narration: Try it this week: pick a problem near you, like a tank that runs dry or a hot classroom. Draw your design as four boxes: sense, decide, act, connect. Score two designs, then ask someone at home what you missed.

checkpoints.prompt: The bridge's water sensor breaks during a storm. What should the warning light do?

options.text: Flash, and report that it's broken
Stay off until someone fixes it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a broken sensor must never look like “all clear”. When in doubt, warn, and call for repair.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a dark light tells drivers “safe to cross”. A good design fails safe: when it can't tell, it warns.

checkpoints.prompt: Grace's design scores best, but she never asked the minibus drivers. What should she do before building it?

options.text: Build it now: the scores are clear
Show the drivers and ask what she missed

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the drivers know things her scores can't show, like when and how they could read an alert.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — scores only hold what she thought of. The drivers may know what she missed, so ask before building.
